subject: agriculture
title: Cambridge IGCSE Agriculture (0600)

officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and subtopic headings and their numbers (1 to 10, 1.1 to 10.5) are transcribed from the subject content of the official syllabus; objective codes are the syllabus's own content letters (for example 2.3(e)). The node 7.0 'Study of one ruminant and one non-ruminant' and its objective are ours, built from the sentence that introduces topic 7. Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase; no syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Read 2026-10-08 from the official PDF (version 1, published September 2024, for exams in 2027 and 2028; November series only; not available in all administrative zones): the ten topics, every numbered subtopic and content item, the assessment overview, the details of the assessment and the list of changes ('no significant changes which affect teaching').

This version is examined from 2027. A student sitting the examination in 2026 is examined on the previous syllabus version, which is not in the repository; because the list of changes reports no significant changes to teaching, the content is expected to match. The 2027-2028 version is published as the current version because new students now will sit 2027 or later.

Assessment as read: Paper 1 Theory (1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, 70%, externally assessed): Section A, 70 marks, short-answer and structured questions, all compulsory; Section B, two of five free-response structured questions of 15 marks each (30 marks). Component 2 Practical Coursework (90 marks, 30%, internally assessed and externally moderated): four practical exercises of 15 marks each (60 marks; criteria responsibility, initiative, technique, perseverance and quality, 3 marks each) and one practical investigation reported in no more than 1000 words (30 marks). Calculators may be used in all parts of the assessment. Grades A* to G; no tiers. AO weightings: AO1 30%, AO2 40%, AO3 30% overall (Paper 1: AO1 45%, AO2 55%).

The number and marks of Section A questions are not given in the syllabus; the mock convention of seven 10-mark structured questions is ours and should be checked against the specimen paper. The content overview names topic 10 'Farm structure and tools'; the subject content heading 'Farm structures and tools' is used here.

Not in this syllabus (taught in the family for ZIMSEC only): land tenure and land reform, natural farming regions, adverse-condition modification and natural disasters, forestry, wildlife, water conservation and harvesting, irrigation equipment, water pollution and legislation, respiration and tropisms, vegetable and orchard production, types of livestock, poultry reproduction, layers and indigenous chickens, rabbits, donkeys, mitosis and meiosis, harnesses, pumps and shellers, farm roads, profit and loss accounts, budgets and gross margins, agricultural marketing and co-operatives. Component 2 coursework is not simulated.
overview: Cambridge IGCSE Agriculture is an applied, practical science course in ten topics: general agriculture (land use and agricultural economics), soil (formation, properties, fertility, erosion, drainage, irrigation and the water cycle), principles of plant growth, crop production, crop protection, livestock anatomy and physiology, livestock production and health, pasture management, livestock and crop breeding, and farm structures and tools.
assessmentOverview: All candidates take Paper 1 Theory (1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, 70%: Section A 70 marks of compulsory short-answer and structured questions; Section B two 15-mark questions from a choice of five) and Component 2 Practical Coursework (90 marks, 30%: four practical exercises and a practical investigation, internally assessed and externally moderated). Calculators may be used.

components.name: Paper 1: Theory
components.description: Section A (70 marks): compulsory short-answer and structured questions. Section B (30 marks): two free-response structured questions of 15 marks each from a choice of five.

components.name: Component 2: Practical Coursework
components.description: Four practical exercises (60 marks) and one practical investigation with a written report (30 marks), internally assessed and externally moderated.

objectives.text: Describe forms of land use, including agricultural systems and practices (rotations, mixed farming, monoculture), forestry and aquaculture.
Describe and explain how topography, climate and other environmental factors limit land use in different areas.
Understand that population growth requires efficient land use and farm planning.
Describe organic production, hydroponics and GM crops and discuss the arguments for and against GM crops and organic production.
Explain supply and demand, diminishing returns, the opportunities and choices facing farmers and decision making based on economic factors.
Explain how soil forms from parent material by physical, chemical and biological weathering.

children.name: Soil types, composition, texture and temperature

objectives.text: Describe the soil profile: topsoil, subsoil and underlying material.
Describe soil texture in terms of sand, silt and clay particle sizes.
Understand soil structure: forming and keeping a good crumb structure, the role of humus and organic matter, and how oxidation of organic matter leads to capping and soil pans.
Describe sandy, loam and clay soils and their properties, including water-holding capacity and drainage.
Outline soil constituents: mineral matter, organic matter, air, water (gravitational, capillary, hygroscopic) and living organisms.
Understand how soil temperature affects plant growth, the dangers of excessive heat and frost, and how mulching and shading reduce extremes.
Explain the importance of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulfur and describe the signs and effects of their deficiency.
Carry out soil sampling and soil pH tests.
Describe the nitrogen cycle and its importance to soil fertility.
Explain the importance of legumes, manure and compost in maintaining soil structure and fertility.
Describe the use of inorganic fertilisers (one mainly phosphorus, one mainly potassium and one compound fertiliser).
Explain how fertilising and liming affect soil pH.
Describe the types, causes and agents of soil erosion and its prevention and control.
Describe drainage as the downward movement of gravitational water, the draining of waterlogged land by ditches and the loss of nutrients by leaching.
Understand the effects of poor drainage on soil organisms and root respiration.
Explain the need for irrigation and describe irrigation methods and their effects on crop yield and quality (no crop programmes or equipment specifications).
Describe the water cycle and ground-water resources and their significance.
Describe the distribution and function of root tissues and the structure and function of root hairs.
Explain the absorption of water and mineral salts by diffusion and osmosis and their passage through vascular tissue.
Explain how leaf structure is related to function (no cellular detail).
Outline gas exchange by diffusion through stomata.
Describe photosynthesis in terms of carbon dioxide, water, light and chlorophyll producing carbohydrates and oxygen.
Describe the distribution and function of tissues in a dicotyledonous stem.
Define translocation and explain how plant parts are modified as food storage organs and the foods they store.
Explain transpiration: the transpiration stream, evaporation and diffusion of water vapour through stomata.
Describe the effects of temperature, humidity, wind and light intensity on transpiration.
Define sexual reproduction.
Describe the structure and functions of maize and bean flowers.
Define pollination.
Describe fertilisation in a named plant.
Describe seed and fruit dispersal and explain its importance in weed control.
Describe asexual reproduction from stem tubers and stem cuttings.
Describe seed structure and germination of maize and a legume and the conditions for germination.
Describe stumping and clearing and primary and secondary cultivation by hand or machine.
Name the main types of crop grown locally (legumes, roots and tubers, fruits, cereals) and their products.

Describe in detail the cultivation of one crop of local importance: requirements, soil preparation, sowing, cultivars, seed rate and spacing, fertiliser and manure rates, pest, weed and disease control, maturity, harvesting, yield, storage and record keeping.
Identify one named local weed of a crop and describe its harmful effects and mode of spread.
Explain cultural, mechanical and chemical methods of weed control.
Describe the life cycle, effect and spread of one biting and chewing pest, one piercing and sucking pest and one boring pest.
Name and describe the mode of action of contact and systemic pesticides and their appropriate use.
Describe biological and biotechnical methods of pest control.
Describe cultural pest control, including rotation and catch cropping.
Describe the infection, harmful effects, prevention and control of one named bacterial, one fungal and one viral plant disease.
Explain safe handling of farm chemicals: protective clothing, dilution and mixing, precautions before, during and after use, and avoiding pollution when cleaning sprayers.
Explain the safe storage of toxic chemicals and flammable fuels.
Describe the structure and function of the digestive systems of a ruminant and a non-ruminant.
Describe digestion and absorption in a ruminant and a non-ruminant (no enzymes).
Describe the male and female reproductive systems of a named farm mammal.
Describe fertilisation and birth in a named farm mammal.
Define weaning and lactation and understand the importance of colostrum.

topics.name: Livestock production and health
topics.description: The syllabus asks for the study of one ruminant and one non-ruminant with particular reference to housing, nutrition and health. The node 'Study of one ruminant and one non-ruminant' is ours and holds the species concepts.

children.name: Study of one ruminant and one non-ruminant
children.description: Our node (code ours): the named animals studied under 7.1 to 7.3.

objectives.text: Apply the housing, nutrition and health content of 7.1 to 7.3 to one named ruminant and one named non-ruminant (our objective).
Describe suitable housing and living conditions for livestock.
Describe the care and rearing of young stock.
Describe nutritional requirements, deficiency signs and feeding practices, including balanced rations for the age and stage of the animal.
Outline maintenance and production rations.
Explain the importance of an adequate, clean water supply.
Demonstrate stockmanship: careful handling of animals and keeping a diary of events and production records.
Recognise signs of health and ill-health in livestock.
Explain how infectious and contagious diseases spread.
Explain the problems caused by parasites.
Explain notifiable (scheduled) diseases.
Explain the importance of hygiene and isolating sick animals.
Describe the vegetation of grazing lands: grasses and legumes for grazing and bush for browsing.
Describe how improved pastures are established.
Explain rotational, paddock and zero grazing, enclosed and unenclosed systems and intensive and extensive grazing.
Describe extensive management: stocking rates, carrying capacity, overstocking, bush control and the use and misuse of fire.
Explain how fencing and rotational grazing improve pasture use.
Define chromosome, gene, allele, homozygous, heterozygous, dominant and recessive.
Calculate and predict the results of monohybrid crosses giving 1:1 and 3:1 ratios.
Explain genotype and phenotype and their importance in animal and plant breeding.

children.name: Selective breeding in animals and plants

objectives.text: Describe how breeding improves yield, disease resistance, hardiness and appearance in livestock and crops.
Understand the role of artificial selection in producing improved varieties.
Understand the benefits of artificial insemination.
Understand the differences between selective crop breeding and GM crops.
Describe the treatment of fencing posts, fence construction, types of fence for different purposes, and hedges and windbreaks.
Outline the properties and uses of wood, concrete blocks, metal, stone, brick, earth and thatch in farm buildings.
List sources of water for people, livestock and irrigation.
Outline water treatment by settling and filtration.
Outline the construction of storage dams that resist water pressure, which increases with depth.
Describe storage tanks, pipe distribution and simple plumbing, including joining pipes and fitting tap washers.
Describe the use and maintenance of a saw, hammer, screwdriver, file, spanner, sprayers and hand tools for cultivation.
Explain the advantages and disadvantages of farm mechanisation.
Describe the use and maintenance of the mouldboard plough, cultivator, harrow, planter and ridger (ox-, donkey- or tractor-drawn).
